Photoreal live-action. Midday samurai duel, and this is the sequence where the fight is most visible in the whole film, on purpose: the more of the duel you see, the less of it you understand. Cinematography: high hard midday light, very short shadows sitting directly under the brow and the jaw, strong contrast, deep closed blacks, no soft fill anywhere.

SPEED LAW — CRITICAL, READ THIS FIRST: this fight is FAST and RELENTLESS. Real-time 24fps, and if anything a shade faster than life, never slower. No speed ramps, no slow-motion impacts, no lingering on a blow, no beat held for effect. NO ROOM TO BREATHE: no shot ever ends on a pause, a recovery or a held pose while steel is in frame. Every such shot ends INTO the next attack with a body already moving. The men do not reset between exchanges, do not step back to admire, do not lower their blades. The moment steel leaves steel the next attack is already loading.

STRIKE LAW: every cut is ONE violent committed movement, not a demonstration. The blade arrives and CONTINUES OUT the other side in the same motion, finishing in the air past the body. It never stops on a body, never rests on skin or cloth, never pauses at the moment of contact. DO NOT break a cut into stages and DO NOT show the wind-up as a separate beat: the hips and the blade go together and the whole thing is over in a fraction of a second. NOBODY EVER PRESENTS A BODY PART TO A BLADE. The man who is struck is always mid-defence, his own blade already moving to intercept, beaten late by a hand's width. Nothing waits, nothing poses, nothing holds still to be hit.

SWORDSMANSHIP LAW, this is Japanese swordsmanship and it must read as such: GRIP, the tell that gives away a fake: the two hands are APART on the hilt, the left hand at the very end of the grip and the right hand just under the guard, with a gap of two fists between them. Never both hands together like a baseball bat. CUT: driven by the hips turning and the LEFT hand pulling down, never by the arms throwing the blade. An arm-thrown cut looks like an axe swing and is wrong. GUARDS: middle guard, point at the opponent's throat, hands at navel height. High guard, blade lifted above the head. Low guard, point dropped toward the opponent's knees. FOOTWORK: inside striking distance the steps SLIDE, right foot leading, heels never fully down, feet NEVER crossing. Nobody jumps and nobody lunges like a fencer. DISTANCE: they open and close the gap constantly. They never stand planted trading blows.

FIGHTER LAW: when a blade reaches a swordsman he IS CUT, and the film shows it. His CLOTH SPLITS OPEN along the blade's path with torn edges lifting, and underneath it a clean line opens in his SKIN, exactly where the edge passed. ★ THE RITE — CRITICAL — THIS IS WHY IT HAPPENS, AND IT MUST BE VISIBLE AND AUDIBLE: every kneeling man is CHANTING, continuously, from the moment he kneels until the duel ends, and the chant is what moves the wound from one body to the other. This is not invisible magic, it is a rite being worked by a man doing his job. HOW IT LOOKS: his lips move constantly but barely, a few millimetres, the jaw working low and steady, the throat moving. No shouting, no wide mouth, no theatrical incantation, no raised hands, no gesture, no eyes rolled back, no swaying. He is looking at the sand in front of his own knees the whole time. It reads as a working man repeating something he has repeated a thousand times, never as a priest performing. HOW IT SOUNDS: one low sustained syllable on the breath, repeated on a monotone, barely above a whisper, sitting UNDER the wind in the mix. No melody, no rhythm, no words a viewer could read or repeat, no choir, no harmony, no added reverb, no second voice. Never translated and never subtitled. WHEN A CUT LANDS ON HIM the chant CATCHES for a fraction of a second, on the same frame the line opens, and then resumes at exactly the same pitch and speed. It never becomes a cry and it never gets louder. IF A KNEELING MAN STOPS CHANTING, THE TRANSFER STOPS. That is the rule the whole film is built on: standing up is only the visible half of stopping.

SHOT 1 — 0–4s — THE CHARGE AND THE BIND

35mm spherical prime, chest-height camera, lateral handheld side-tracking, approximately 5 metres from the fighters.

THIS SHOT ONLY is slow motion.

Both swordsmen are already fully visible in the first frame, sixteen metres apart at opposite ends of the raked sand.

They launch toward each other at the exact same instant.

Not an athletic sprint. A swordsman’s charge: bodies low and level, almost no vertical bounce, eyes locked, both hands on the hilt, blades carried low along the right side, arms never pumping.

The camera RUNS WITH THEM laterally.

Sand detonates under every step and hangs glowing in the hard low sun.

The distance collapses fast.

Their final two strides become sliding sword steps.

Both bodies sink lower.

At the instant the blades meet, playback SNAPS to full real-time speed.

Steel collides violently edge-to-edge into a hard bind.

The camera physically jolts from the impact.

Sand jumps.

The shock travels visibly through both men’s arms into their shoulders.

Faces remain fully readable in frame, separated by less than a hand.

### MAIN CHARACTERS

Feature these two protagonists clearly and powerfully:

The poster must instantly communicate the central concept:
**one man fights, the other carries the wounds.**

Make **<<<0f281e8c-71f7-40e9-96f1-1e0ebd970493>>>** the emotional center of the poster.

**the kneeling man suffers, the standing man remains uncut.**

* low cold morning light
* pine trees at the perimeter
* harsh natural atmosphere
* dust and faint wind
* austere ritual space
* maybe distant blurred witnesses at the far edge, but they should not distract

### TONE

The mood must be:

* mythic but grounded
* emotionally heavy
* visually elegant
* prestige historical drama
* brutal loyalty
* ancient ritual
* quiet horror

### LIGHTING

Naturalistic cinematic dawn lighting:

* tactile skin texture and fabric texture

### CAMERA / POSTER FEEL

FRAMING LAW: a fighter's head is never cropped by any edge. Duel framing runs from mid-thigh to a hand's width above the head, so legs, torso, the crossing blades and BOTH FACES sit in the same frame. Kneeling framing runs from the knees to above the head. NEVER legs alone, NEVER feet alone, NEVER an empty landscape with nobody in it.

LOOK: one rule governs every frame, a world with no colour in it and one saturated colour that lives only in cloth, 90 to 10. The 90 carries no chroma: pale raked sand, undyed linen, dark robes and the pine line read as one neutral scale from bone white to near-black. The 10 is the deep madder red of set-in staining in cloth. Skin keeps its own low warmth. No fourth colour.

LIGHT: natural daylight only, one source and it is the low early sun, just risen, out of frame to the left behind the pine trunks so its disc is never seen. It rakes almost horizontally: every pine throws a shadow ten metres long across the sand and the trunks cut the light into bright bars and dark bars. Warm low sun on what it touches, cold blue open shade on what it misses, four stops between the two. Low mist between the trunks so the beams read. No fill, no rim light, no lens flare.

GLASS: spherical primes, f/2.8, physical cine lens, 180 degree shutter motion blur, fine 35mm grain, no halation. Depth of field exactly as the declared focal length at f/2.8 behaves: sharp on the declared subject distance and falling off progressively behind it, never blurred harder than that lens could blur it and never everything sharp at once.
